title: Bullous Keratopathy: Unveiling the Cornea's Edematous Distress
summary: Bullous keratopathy (BK) is a chronic, progressive corneal condition characterized by dysfunction or loss of corneal endothelial cells. This leads to persistent stromal and epithelial edema, vision loss, and ocular discomfort. While often surgically managed with corneal transplantation, recent advances offer hope for targeted therapies and regeneration.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Bullous keratopathy (BK) refers to a chronic, progressive corneal edema caused by dysfunction or loss of corneal endothelial cells. This leads to a failure of the endothelial pump mechanism, resulting in excessive fluid accumulation within the corneal stroma and epithelium. Clinically, it manifests as epithelial microcysts, bullae, and eventual subepithelial fibrosis, causing significant vision impairment and ocular discomfort.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology & Risk Factors
content: Incidence: Varies globally; Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy (PBK) is a leading indication for corneal transplantation worldwide, accounting for 20-30% of penetrating keratoplasties and 50-60% of endothelial keratoplasties.
Prevalence: Increases with age due to age-related endothelial cell loss and prevalence of cataract surgery.
Risk Factors:
Intraocular Surgery: Cataract extraction (especially complicated cases, prolonged phaco time, posterior capsular rupture, vitreous loss, anterior chamber IOLs, retained lens fragments).
Fuchs' Endothelial Dystrophy (FED): Pre-existing endothelial disease.
Intraocular Lens (IOL) Factors: Malpositioned IOLs, haptic-endothelium touch, IOL subluxation/dislocation.
Trauma: Direct endothelial damage, chemical injury.
Glaucoma: Chronic high intraocular pressure, glaucoma surgery (e.g., trabeculectomy with bleb-cornea touch), acute angle closure.
Uveitis: Chronic inflammation affecting endothelium.
Hereditary: Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy (CHED).

sections.title: 3. Etiology & Pathophysiology: The Endothelial Pump Failure

branches: Loss of Endothelial Cells (e.g., age, trauma, surgery)
Inflow > Outflow of Aqueous into Stroma
Result: Stromal & Epithelial Edema → Bullae Formation

rows: Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy (PBK)
Corneal edema following cataract surgery with IOL implantation.
Surgical trauma, IOL-endothelium touch, pre-existing subclinical FED.
Aphakic Bullous Keratopathy (ABK)
Corneal edema following cataract surgery without IOL implantation (historical, less common).
Surgical trauma, absence of protective IOL, pre-existing endothelial issues.
Fuchs' Endothelial Dystrophy (FED)
Primary, bilateral, inherited endothelial dystrophy with guttae formation.
Genetic predisposition (e.g., TCF4 gene), age-related endothelial cell loss.
Other Causes
Edema due to other ocular conditions.
Trauma, uveitis, glaucoma, CHED, chemical injury.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Patient Symptoms
content: Gradual decline in vision (especially in mornings due to epithelial edema, clearing throughout day).
Ocular pain (due to bullae rupture, exposure of nerve endings).
Photophobia (light sensitivity).
Foreign body sensation.
Epiphora (tearing).
Halos around lights.
Redness (secondary inflammation or infection).

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings (Slit-Lamp)
content: Epithelium:
Microcystic edema (fine refractile dots).
Epithelial bullae (fluid-filled blisters), often rupturing to form erosions.
Subepithelial fibrosis (in chronic cases, grey-white opacities).
Stroma:
Stromal edema (thickened cornea, loss of transparency, stromal folds).
Descemet's folds (vertical or horizontal wrinkles).
Endothelium:
Cornea guttae (Fuchs' dystrophy, seen as 'beaten bronze' appearance).
Reduced endothelial cell density (difficult to appreciate clinically without specular microscopy).
Other:
Mild anterior chamber reaction (if associated with inflammation).
Stromal neovascularization (rare, in chronic cases with severe inflammation).
IOL position and integrity (for PBK).

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Comprehensive Ophthalmic History & Exam: Assess visual acuity, pain, photophobia. Slit-lamp exam to evaluate corneal layers, IOP, IOL status.
Step 2: Corneal Pachymetry: Measures corneal thickness (CCT). Edematous corneas are significantly thicker (>600 µm, normal 500-550 µm).
Step 3: Specular Microscopy/Confocal Microscopy:
Specular Microscopy: Quantifies endothelial cell density (ECD) and analyzes cell morphology (polymegathism, pleomorphism). ECD <1000 cells/mm² is often a critical threshold for developing edema.
Confocal Microscopy: Provides in-vivo imaging of all corneal layers, including endothelial cells, to assess morphology and identify guttae.

Step 4: Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT): Visualizes corneal edema, epithelial and stromal thickening, presence of bullae, and Descemet's membrane abnormalities. Useful for pre-operative planning for endothelial keratoplasty.
Step 5: Fundus Examination: Rule out other posterior segment pathology, especially if vision loss is disproportionate.

rows: Acute Hydrops (Keratoconus)
Sudden, painful vision loss in a known keratoconus patient; rupture of Descemet's, severe stromal edema, sometimes white scar. Usually unilateral and acute.
Tends to resolve over weeks-months with topical steroids, cycloplegics; often requires PKP later.
Infectious Keratitis (Bacterial/Fungal)
Pain, redness, discharge, epithelial defect with stromal infiltrate, sometimes hypopyon. Culture positive.
Aggressive antimicrobial therapy. May progress to perforation.
Other Corneal Dystrophies
Posterior Polymorphous Dystrophy (PPMD), Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy (CHED). Characteristic slit-lamp signs (vesicles, band-like lesions in PPMD, diffuse haziness in CHED).
Specific genetic testing for CHED. Endothelial keratoplasty for advanced cases.
Chemical Injury
History of exposure, limbal ischemia, corneal opacification, inflammation.
Emergency irrigation, steroids, amniotic membrane, limbal stem cell transplant.
Uveitis-related Keratopathy
Presence of anterior chamber inflammation (cells, flare, keratic precipitates).
Treat underlying uveitis with steroids, cycloplegics.

sections.title: 9. Staging / Progression of Bullous Keratopathy
content: Stage 1: Mild Edema
Subclinical endothelial dysfunction.
Slight increase in corneal thickness (measured by pachymetry).
Early guttae formation (in FED).
Morning vision fluctuation.
Stage 2: Epithelial Microcysts & Bullae
Visible epithelial edema and microcysts.
Small, fragile epithelial bullae.
Moderate vision reduction, mild discomfort.
Stage 3: Ruptured Bullae & Persistent Epithelial Erosions
Recurrent episodes of bullae rupture leading to painful erosions.
Increased photophobia, foreign body sensation.
Risk of secondary infection.
Stage 4: Subepithelial Fibrosis & Scarring
Chronic inflammation and healing leads to subepithelial scarring.
Reduced transparency, irreversible vision loss.
Pain may lessen if nerve endings become scarred, but vision remains poor.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Algorithm
content: Step 1: Conservative/Medical Management (for mild-moderate symptoms or temporary relief):
Hypertonic Saline: Topical 5% NaCl drops (e.g., Muro 128) 4-6 times daily, ointment at night. Draws fluid from cornea by osmosis.
Bandage Contact Lens (BCL): Therapeutic BCLs provide pain relief by protecting exposed nerve endings from ruptured bullae; changed regularly (e.g., weekly or bi-weekly).
Topical Steroids: Low-dose prednisolone acetate 1% or fluorometholone 0.1% qid for short periods if significant inflammation is present, but judicious use due to steroid-induced IOP rise.
IOP Control: If secondary glaucoma, topical anti-glaucoma medications (e.g., timolol, brimonidine, prostaglandin analogues) as needed.
Pain Relief: Oral NSAIDs or topical diclofenac/ketorolac.
Step 2: Surgical Management (for severe symptoms, persistent pain, or significant vision loss):
Endothelial Keratoplasty (EK):

DMEK (Descemet's Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty): Preferred for Fuchs' and PBK due to superior visual outcomes, faster recovery, and lower rejection rates. Involves selective transplantation of Descemet's membrane and endothelium.

DSAEK/DSEK (Descemet's Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty): Involves transplantation of Descemet's membrane, endothelium, and a thin layer of posterior stroma. Easier technically than DMEK, good visual outcomes.

Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): Full-thickness corneal transplant. Reserved for cases with significant stromal scarring, peripheral involvement, or when EK is not suitable (e.g., very thin corneas, complex anterior segment).
Amniotic Membrane Transplantation (AMT): Can be used for persistent epithelial defects or pain control in severe cases, but not a definitive treatment for edema.
Step 3: Advanced & Experimental Treatments:
Rho-kinase (ROCK) inhibitors (e.g., Netarsudil, Ripasudil) – promotes endothelial cell migration and proliferation.
Corneal endothelial cell injection therapy.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: Endothelial Keratoplasty Focus
content: DMEK (Descemet's Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty):
Step 1: Donor Preparation: A very thin (10-15 µm) Descemet's membrane with endothelium is peeled from a cadaveric donor cornea. Often pre-stripped ('pre-DMEK').
Step 2: Recipient Preparation: The diseased Descemet's membrane is stripped from the recipient cornea (Descemetorhexis) through a small limbal incision (2.4-3.0mm).
Step 3: Graft Insertion: The scrolled donor graft is inserted into the anterior chamber via an injector.

Step 4: Graft Unfurling & Attachment: The graft is carefully unfurled and positioned centrally, then secured against the host stroma using an anterior chamber air bubble. Patient remains supine for a few hours post-op.
DSAEK/DSEK (Descemet's Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty):
Step 1: Donor Preparation: A microkeratome or femtosecond laser is used to create a posterior stromal lamellar graft (100-200 µm thick) from a donor cornea.
Step 2: Recipient Preparation: Recipient Descemet's membrane is stripped.
Step 3: Graft Insertion: The thicker donor lenticule is folded or inserted via an injector into the anterior chamber.
Step 4: Graft Attachment: An air bubble is used to secure the graft. Less prone to folding than DMEK.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: Complications of EK (DMEK/DSAEK):
Graft detachment (most common, requires re-bubbling: ~5-15%).
Graft rejection (lower with DMEK/DSAEK than PKP, ~1-5%).
Primary graft failure (due to poor donor quality or surgical trauma).
Infection (endophthalmitis, rare).
Pupillary block glaucoma (due to air bubble).
IOP spikes.
Cataract progression.
Complications of PKP:
Graft rejection (higher, ~10-20%).
Astigmatism (significant, often requiring rigid gas permeable lenses).
Infection, glaucoma, suture-related complications.

Prognosis: Excellent with successful EK; most patients achieve 20/40 or better vision. PKP also has good outcomes but longer visual recovery and higher complication rates. Untreated, BK leads to chronic pain and severe vision loss.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: Sudden, severe increase in pain or vision loss post-operatively (suggests acute graft detachment, infection, or pupillary block).
Presence of purulent discharge or significant anterior chamber inflammation (suggests endophthalmitis or severe infection).
Progressive corneal opacification despite treatment (may indicate advanced disease or treatment failure).
Acute, painful red eye with reduced vision in a patient with a BCL (consider contact lens-related infection/ulcer).

content.explanation: Fuchs' Dystrophy, Aphakic/Pseudophakic Keratopathy, Trauma (surgical, chemical), Hydrops (acute), Endothelialitis (inflammatory), Raised IOP (glaucoma)

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls for Bullous Keratopathy
content: Morning blurry vision that improves during the day is a hallmark symptom due to overnight accumulation of epithelial edema.
Corneal pachymetry is a simple, non-invasive tool to objectively monitor corneal edema.
Specular microscopy is crucial for pre-operative assessment of endothelial cell health and guiding surgical decisions.
DMEK offers faster visual recovery and lower rejection rates compared to DSAEK and PKP, making it the preferred choice for suitable cases.
Persistent epithelial defects in BK are painful and increase the risk of infectious keratitis; BCLs and hypertonic saline are essential for management.
Always check IOL position in PBK to rule out haptic-endothelium touch or IOL subluxation.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Future Directions
content: Rho-Kinase (ROCK) Inhibitors: Topical Ripasudil (approved in Japan for FED) and Netarsudil (approved for glaucoma, shows promise in stimulating endothelial cell proliferation and adhesion, especially in FED). Currently off-label use for BK.

Corneal Endothelial Cell Injection Therapy: Cultured human corneal endothelial cells (HCECs) injected into the anterior chamber, often with a ROCK inhibitor, to repopulate the endothelium. Clinical trials underway (e.g., Shirasawa et al. in Japan). This represents a potential paradigm shift from transplantation to regeneration.
Ultrathin DSAEK (UT-DSAEK): Further reduction of graft thickness improves visual outcomes, bridging the gap towards DMEK.
Femtosecond Laser-Assisted EK: Potential for more precise and reproducible graft preparation.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
sections.content:
Bullous keratopathy is rare in the pediatric population. When present, it is typically associated with:

Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy (CHED): A bilateral, genetically inherited condition causing corneal clouding from birth or early infancy. Requires early PKP or EK (DMEK possible even in children) for visual rehabilitation.
Complicated Pediatric Cataract Surgery: Although rare, severe surgical trauma in an infant eye can lead to endothelial decompensation.
Trauma: Especially chemical injuries.
Glaucoma: Uncontrolled congenital glaucoma can lead to corneal edema.

Management in children requires careful consideration of amblyopia prevention and appropriate anesthetic and surgical techniques suitable for smaller eyes.
